what_it_does: Before a chip design is manufactured, engineers must verify that two versions of a circuit (say, before and after a design tool optimized it) produce identical outputs for every possible input — a task called combinational equivalence checking (CEC). The standard approach uses a mathematical technique called SAT solving (satisfiability solving), which can bog down or time out on very large circuits. This paper explores using a GPU — the same massively parallel graphics processor used for AI training — to instead run enormous numbers of simulated test patterns through both circuit versions simultaneously, checking whether any input ever causes a mismatch. Because GPUs can run thousands of computations at once, this simulation-based approach reportedly achieves an 88x speedup over a CPU SAT solver on large test cases. When simulation alone is not enough to reach a definitive answer, the method falls back to a conventional SAT tool. The specific conditions under which this hybrid approach succeeds or fails are detailed in the full paper.
